## Hybrids in practice

The first large hybrid was Jamba from AI21, in March 2024: Mamba layers with one attention layer in every eight<sup>[14]</sup>. MiniMax, NVIDIA, Qwen and Moonshot followed, each with its own recurrent layer and its own ratio.

MiniMax-Text-01 put one softmax layer after every seven layers of lightning attention, a fast form of linear attention, after finding that lightning attention alone “demonstrates limited retrieval capabilities”<sup>[15]</sup>. NVIDIA’s Nemotron-H models keep “roughly 8% of the total number of layers” as attention, and the rest are Mamba-2 and MLP layers<sup>[16]</sup>.

Qwen3-Next uses Gated DeltaNet in three layers out of four. According to the Qwen team, at this ratio “the model consistently outperforms any monolithic architecture”<sup>[17]</sup>.

Kimi Linear uses Kimi Delta Attention, the variant with a gate for every channel, also at 3:1. It leaves word order entirely to the recurrent layers: its attention layers use no positional encoding at all<sup>[9]</sup>.

Here is where each model keeps its full attention, read from the config files the models are published with:


Drawn to scale, the designs differ more than their headline ratios. Jamba and MiniMax-Text-01 keep one attention layer in eight, Nemotron-H-8B 4 of its 28 token-mixing layers, the Qwen and Kimi models one in four.

Kimi Linear’s released model has 27 layers, so its 3:1 turns into 20 recurrent layers and 7 attention layers, the last one attention.

Kimi K3, 93 layers deep, adds an extra attention layer at the top, “ensuring that the final layer always performs global attention”<sup>[18]</sup>. All of them spread the attention layers evenly through the depth.

The second group shrinks the cache in another way. gpt-oss and Gemma use softmax attention in every layer, but most of their layers see only a sliding window of recent tokens: 128 in gpt-oss, where windowed and full layers alternate<sup>[19]</sup>, and 1,024 in Gemma 3, with five windowed layers for every full one<sup>[20]</sup>.

At 128 pairs even the Transformer didn’t learn the task in 4,000 steps, which is why the chart stops at 64.

Gated DeltaNet, the newest of the three, comes last from 16 pairs on. That is less strange than it looks, because this test gives the gate nothing to do. Every pair has to be kept until its question comes, so forgetting can only lose information.

The authors of Gated DeltaNet, who trained models of 1.3 billion parameters on 100 billion tokens of real text, found that it “consistently surpasses existing models like Mamba2 and DeltaNet”, in-context retrieval included<sup>[8]</sup>. Four layers and 4,000 steps of a synthetic task are a different regime.

Trap

The gate is the easiest part to get wrong. In my first version it started at about one half, and weight decay kept pulling it back there, so the state lost half of what it held at every token, and Gated DeltaNet and the hybrid stayed at chance level. Starting the gate as the Gated DeltaNet and Mamba-2 code does, where a typical head keeps about 94% of its state from one token to the next, and leaving it out of weight decay, fixed it.

The two hybrids differ only in the order of their layers. With attention second, the hybrid recalls every value at every size, like the Transformer, though three of its four layers are Gated DeltaNet, which on its own recalls the least.

With attention on top, the same layers recall 26% of the values at 16 pairs and 12% at 32, at the better of two learning rates: a little more than Gated DeltaNet alone and less than DeltaNet.

I can’t say for certain why. The attention layer on top has what it needs: the convolution hands each value its key, and the other hybrid shows that one attention layer among three Gated DeltaNet layers is enough. This one just doesn’t learn the lookup in 4,000 steps.

A model of four layers is far from Qwen3-Next, where twelve attention layers are spread through 48 and most of them have many recurrent layers on both sides, so this says nothing about whether its layout is a good one.

Gemma 4 kept the ratio. A window is the opposite trade to a recurrent state: it keeps recent tokens exactly and forgets older ones completely, while a state keeps a blurred summary of everything.

The last row is MiniMax-M2, the successor of MiniMax-Text-01, with full attention in all 62 layers. The team explained why in a blog post.

Small hybrids had matched full attention on the leaderboards, but “the price paid became obvious at a larger scale: the model had clear deficits in complex, multi-hop reasoning tasks”<sup>[21]</sup>.

The Qwen and Kimi hybrids keep more attention than MiniMax-Text-01 did, one layer in four rather than one in eight, and use the delta rule, which lightning attention lacks. Still, the episode is a fair warning that parity on small models and leaderboards doesn’t settle the question.

What the hybrids save is easiest to see in memory. For each model, the size of its cache follows from the config: the number of attention layers, key-value heads and head dimension.


For one sequence of 128K tokens, Qwen3-Next keeps 3 GiB of keys and values, against 32 GiB for Qwen3-32B. Not all of the factor of ten comes from the hybrid. Each attention layer of Qwen3-Next keeps two key-value heads of 256 dimensions, where Qwen3-32B keeps eight of 128, which halves the cache per layer.

The rest, a factor of 5.3, is 12 attention layers instead of 64. The recurrent layers add a state of 36 MiB that stays the same at any length.

Kimi Linear starts from multi-head latent attention, introduced in DeepSeek-V2<sup>[22]</sup>, which already caches one compressed vector of 576 numbers per token and layer in place of keys and values for every head, and keeps it in 7 layers of 27.

That is 26% of the cache of an all-MLA model of the same depth, in line with the paper’s “reducing KV cache usage by up to 75%”. MiniMax-M2, at 31 GiB, keeps six times more than its predecessor.

At long context, the cache rather than the weights decides how many conversations fit on a GPU at once, and decoding speed follows from that.

## III. The Real Bottlenecks

To build a model that can practically be deployed and used by the community, we have to start with what users care: Quality, Speed (TPS), and Price. Quality is non-negotiable. A useless model is useless even if it's free. So how do we make a Linear/Sparse/Hybrid Attention model that performs well enough? The biggest challenge here isn't the architecture design — the real bottleneck is the limitations of evaluation. (As for speed and price, those are heavily influenced by the inference stack—and great models tend to attract great engineers to optimize them.)

### The Evaluation Trap: Goodhart's Law in Action

“As long as you build the benchmark, I'll find a way to beat it.” Over the past few years of LLM development, the pace of leaderboard progress is staggering. No matter how hard a benchmark is — even if the SOTA score starts in single digits — once it catches the industry's attention, it's usually crushed within a few iterations. But how do you build an evaluation system that is comprehensive and actually reflects a model's true capabilities? That's one of the hardest — and most critical — problems in LLM development, and it becomes even more acute when you start messing with a component as fundamental as attention.
### Benchmarks are a Leaky Abstraction

There's no free lunch. When you reduce the complexity of attention, you pay a price. The question is, where?

When we were developing MiniMax-Text-01, everyone was still evaluating MMLU, BBH, MATH, and LongBench (all of which are now saturated). From the perspective of a year ago, a hybrid of Lightning Attention and Full Attention looked just as good as pure full attention. Our own small-scale hybrid models confirmed this on the leaderboards. (Did we find a free lunch?)

Not quite. The price paid became obvious at a larger scale: the model had clear deficits in complex, multi-hop reasoning tasks.

Okay, once a problem is exposed, you can fix it. We developed proxy metrics for this specific weakness and iterated until the hybrid model seemed to match MHA. But does that proxy metric still correlate with real-world downstream performance at an even larger scale? Are there other hidden weaknesses? Who knows. We haven't run those experiments yet.

The better the models get, the harder they are to evaluate. But that's a must part of the journey — keep it up, eval teams!

## When a hybrid is the right choice

A hybrid pays off when contexts are long and there are many of them: agents that carry long transcripts of tool calls, reasoning models that write tens of thousands of tokens, questions over long documents, a server holding hundreds of such conversations at once.

There the cache is most of the memory and reading it is most of the decoding time, and cutting it by a factor of four to ten changes how many users one GPU can serve.

At short contexts the gain is smaller than the headlines suggest. According to Qwen, the decoding throughput of Qwen3-Next is nearly 4 times that of Qwen3-32B at 4K tokens and over 10 times beyond 32K<sup>[17]</sup>.

But Qwen3-Next activates 3 billion parameters per token and Qwen3-32B all 32 billion, so the comparison mixes two savings, the mixture of experts and the hybrid, and the blog doesn’t separate them. The hybrid’s share is the part that grows with the context.

The costs are of three kinds. The first is quality on the tasks attention is best at, precise retrieval and multi-hop reasoning over long inputs: the deficits that sent MiniMax back to full attention.

The second is engineering. Recurrent layers need their own kernels, and serving tricks built around a cache of separate tokens get harder when part of the model keeps a state that has absorbed all of them.

Reusing the cache of a shared prompt needs copies of the state saved at chosen positions, and rolling back a rejected speculative token needs the state from a step earlier.

The third is that the field keeps moving. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next replaced the full attention layers of its hybrid with sparse attention<sup>[23]</sup>, and DeepSeek-V4 combines two kinds of compressed attention instead of adding recurrent layers<sup>[24]</sup>. Both directions go after the same cache.

A hybrid’s way is to give most layers a memory of fixed size and to keep a few that can still read every token.

## A test of memory: associative recall

The language modelling loss says little about memory, because much of predicting the next word needs little of it. A more direct test asks a model to remember what it was told. In multi-query associative recall, a sequence lists key-value pairs and then asks for the values of the keys in a shuffled order<sup>[11]</sup>:

```
k1 v1  k2 v2  ...  kN vN   |   q1 a1  q2 a2  ...  qN aN
```
Each $q_i$ is one of the keys, and the model must put the right value after it. It is the skill behind answering a question about a long document, using a name defined forty pages earlier, or calling a function with the arguments described at the top of a prompt.

I trained six small models on it, each with four layers of width 64 and two heads, the same in everything except how their layers mix tokens: softmax attention in all four, linear attention, DeltaNet, Gated DeltaNet, and two hybrids with three Gated DeltaNet layers and one softmax attention layer.

In one hybrid the attention layer is second; in the other it is on top, the place it has in each block of four in Qwen3-Next.

Every layer, attention included, first passes its queries, keys and values through a short convolution over the last four positions, as Mamba and DeltaNet do, so that a value can carry its key with it.

Each model saw 64 fresh random sequences at each of 4,000 steps and was scored on held-out ones. The models with Gated DeltaNet layers trained on an Apple M2, the others on a T4 (code).


The Transformer recalls every value at every size on the chart. The three recurrent models hold up while there are few pairs and fall apart between 8 and 32: at 32 pairs DeltaNet recalls 36% of the values, linear attention 26% and Gated DeltaNet 2%, and at 64 the best of them, DeltaNet, recalls 13%.

Each head here works with keys of 32 numbers, so by the bound from earlier its state holds at most 32 pairs exactly, and at 16 pairs all three are already well short of full recall.

At 128 pairs even the Transformer didn’t learn the task in 4,000 steps, which is why the chart stops at 64.

## Why one layer of attention is enough

Attention solves associative recall in one layer: the query for $k_i$ meets the stored key $k_i$, the softmax puts nearly all the weight on it, and out comes $v_i$, however many pairs came before.

Arora and colleagues proved that attention needs a model dimension independent of the sequence length for this, while the gated convolutions they studied need one that grows with it.

Measuring the gap in quality between the two kinds of models on real text, they found that “82% of the gap is explained by each model’s ability to recall information that is previously mentioned in-context”<sup>[11]</sup>.

Copying gives the same picture. Jelassi and colleagues proved that two layers of attention can copy strings of exponential length, while models with a fixed state are “fundamentally limited by their fixed-size latent state”<sup>[12]</sup>.

None of this requires attention everywhere. Much of predicting the next token is local, or a matter of keeping a running summary of what the text is about, and a gated recurrent layer does that well and cheaply.

Exact lookups into the distant past are rarer, and a layer that can make them serves the whole model: the recurrent layers around it carry the local context, the attention layer finds the match. In the library picture, most floors work from a notebook page, and every few floors someone is allowed into the archive.

The authors of Mamba-2 tried such hybrids and described the division of labour the same way:

 Attention layers act as a retrieval mechanism to quickly refer to previous tokens in the sequence instead of forcing the model to compress all the context to its memory.

Tri Dao and Albert Gu, the authors of Mamba-2


They found that “around 10% of the total number of layers being attention performs best”<sup>[7]</sup>.

A study at NVIDIA trained an 8-billion-parameter Transformer, pure Mamba and Mamba-2 models and a hybrid with 4 attention layers out of 56 on the same data.

The pure Mamba models began to fail at looking up a number in a phone book beyond about 500 tokens. The hybrid exceeded the Transformer on all 12 standard tasks the authors evaluated, by 2.65 points on average<sup>[13]</sup>.

## IV. What's Next

Scaling remains the name of the game, and context scaling is one of the key problems. Longer and longer context length is key in both pre-training and post-training. As GPU compute growth slows while data length keeps increasing, the benefits of linear and sparse attention will gradually emerge. We should start preparing now:

- Better Data: More multimodal, information-rich long-context data.
- Better Evaluation: More informative evaluation system and experimental paradigms to speed up iteration.
- Better Infrastructure: Mature training and inference infrastructure to fully squeeze out GPU potential.

## V. Addendum: the SWA code...

We accidentally left the SWA inference code in the open-source release, and some people asked why it wasn't used in the final model. Simple answer: the performance wasn't good enough.

That experiment was from quite early on, before GPT-OSS was open-sourced (we were pretty surprised to see its structure, by the way). But I can share a brief summary of our failed attempt. We tried adapting CPT into a Hybrid SWA, testing both inter & intra-layer mixing. The motivation for intra-layer mixing was to balance the compute intensity across all layers, which is friendly to both PP in training and PP or AFD during inference. Unfortunately, neither worked. Performance degraded noticeably as context length grew — which is unacceptable in agentic scenarios.

Our analysis showed that many global attention patterns (like retrieval head and induction head) were already established early during pre-training. CPT can hardly adjust those patterns afterwards. You surely can mitigate the issue by using data probes to identify and keep those heads as full attention — but unfortunately, it's nearly impossible to discover them all from human priors.

(And no, this issue isn't related to attention sinks.)

If you're interested in this line of research, I recommend taking a closer look at GPT-OSS, CWM, and Gemma, especially their long-context performance.

Finally, we're hiring! If you want to join us, send your resume to guixianren@minimaxi.com.

# Why Did M2 End Up as a Full Attention Model?

    *On behave of pre-training lead Haohai Sun.*

    *(zhihu.com/question/19653...)*
  

## I. Introduction

    As the lead of MiniMax-M2 pretrain, I've been getting many queries from the community on **"Why did you turn back the clock and go with full attention with MiniMax M2?"** After explaining the backstory in one chat after another, I figured it's time to write down our journey in a blog. Honestly, I could give you the textbook debate. I could talk all afternoon about why you should build linear/sparse attention. Then, I could turn around and talk all afternoon about why you shouldn't. But what's the point of all that hand-waving? The real question is whether you should actually do it.
  

So, let's start with the conclusion: We are always working on it. But in a real-world, industrial-grade system, the truth is that efficient attention still has some way to go before it can definitively beat full attention. As LLMs have evolved, the entire stack has become monstrously complex. We serve more scenarios, and the architecture design trade-offs are exploding: "How does it perform on code and math? What about agent scenarios? How does it handle multimodality? Does long-chain CoT still hold up? Can RL scale on top of it? Are there hidden traps with low-precision compute? How do you implement interleaved thinking, caching, or speculative decoding? ..."

In short, there's a vast difference between the promise on paper and its payoff in production. You only get to claim that payoff after satisfying Condition 1...n and solving Problem 1...n.

A model of four layers is far from Qwen3-Next, where twelve attention layers are spread through 48 and most of them have many recurrent layers on both sides, so this says nothing about whether its layout is a good one.

The ratio alone doesn’t describe a hybrid: with the same layers in a different order, one model recalled every value, like a Transformer, and the other 12% of them at 32 pairs, like a recurrent network.

## What it costs on a GPU

The recurrent layer pays off only where the cache grows large, and a single layer on one GPU shows where that starts.

I timed one layer with 16 heads of 128 dimensions, about the size of a Gated DeltaNet layer in Qwen3-Next, in two situations: reading a prompt of $n$ tokens at once, and writing one new token after $n$ tokens.

Softmax attention runs through PyTorch’s fused attention kernel in half precision. Gated DeltaNet runs my plain-PyTorch chunked version in single precision, a Python loop over chunks of 64. The comparison is tilted against the recurrent layer on purpose: if it wins anyway, it wins on arithmetic, not on engineering.



Reading a prompt, softmax attention is faster up to 8K tokens, which is no surprise: its kernel is one fused program, and mine is a loop. The slopes differ, though.

From 512 to 65,536 tokens, a sequence 128 times longer, the attention layer gets 8,600 times slower and the recurrent one 124 times slower. The curves cross between 8K and 16K tokens, and at 65K the recurrent layer is 4.2 times faster.

Writing a token is where the cache costs most. Attention reads the keys and values of every earlier token, 512 MiB at 65K tokens in this one layer, and its time grows in proportion, from 0.08 ms to 3.7 ms. The recurrent layer updates a state of 1 MiB and takes 0.2 ms at any length; at that size the time is mostly the overhead of launching a few small GPU kernels.

From about 2K tokens on, the recurrent step is faster, and at 65K it is 16 times faster.

On one GPU the recurrent layer overtakes attention from about 2K tokens when writing a token, and between 8K and 16K tokens when reading a prompt.

One layer and one sequence understate the difference in a real server. There, the caches of all the conversations in a batch have to fit in memory at once, so a model whose cache is a quarter or an eighth of the size can serve proportionally more conversations at the same length.

Kimi Linear’s 6.3 times, quoted above, comes from exactly that. The attention layers of a hybrid still pay the full price; three quarters of its layers stop paying it.

Both forms compute the same numbers, only in a different order. In code, the recurrent form loops over positions and the parallel one builds the masked score matrix:

```
def linear_recurrent(q, k, v):
    q, k = feature(q), feature(k)
    state = q.new_zeros(*q.shape[:2], q.shape[-1], v.shape[-1])  # S = sum of k v^T
    norm = q.new_zeros(*q.shape[:2], q.shape[-1])                # z = sum of k
    out = []
    for t in range(q.shape[2]):
        state = state + k[:, :, t, :, None] * v[:, :, t, None, :]
        norm = norm + k[:, :, t]
        out.append(torch.einsum("bhk,bhkv->bhv", q[:, :, t], state)
                   / torch.einsum("bhk,bhk->bh", q[:, :, t], norm)[..., None])
    return torch.stack(out, dim=2)
def linear_attention(q, k, v):
    q, k = feature(q), feature(k)
    causal = torch.ones(q.shape[2], q.shape[2], dtype=torch.bool).tril()
    scores = (q @ k.transpose(-1, -2)).masked_fill(~causal, 0)
    return (scores @ v) / scores.sum(-1, keepdim=True)
```
On random inputs in double precision the two functions agree to about $10^{-15}$, which is rounding error. The recurrent form is how the layer writes text, one token at a time; the parallel form is how it trains, all positions at once.

The parallel form also shows a catch: it still builds an $n \times n$ matrix of scores, because with a causal mask every position needs its own prefix of the sum and the brackets can’t simply move. Training a linear layer efficiently needs a third form, which comes later.

### The High Cost of Knowing Things

For complex reasoning tasks, we can sometimes find early proxy metrics that correlate well with final performance — but not for all tasks (at least, not yet). As tasks get harder, the amount of experiment compute required just to get a statistically significant signal on your metric grows astronomically — which is ironic, since we study efficient attention because compute is limited.

And beyond the academic benchmarks, optimization issues often only surface at scale. You never really know what's going to happen until you scale up. Anyone who read our M1 paper will recall the serious precision issues we hit during RL training — problems that would've been spotted earlier. Going back and analyzing Lightning Attention's numerical convergence with that experience in hand was incredibly clarifying. Discovering the real problems is often far harder than solving them.

### A Symphony of Variables

There are just too many variables in model training. Different architectures behave very differently on different data distributions and with different optimizers. In a world where our data is constantly being updated, an experiment run on last month's data mix might yield the opposite conclusion today.

We can't observe everything perfectly — but we're working on finding more reliable experimental strategies.

### Infrastructure: Where Theory Meets Metal

Compared to full attention, the infrastructure for linear and sparse attention is much less mature. To actually get the promised results, there's still a lot of groundwork to fill in.

Take linear attention for example: If you analyze the compute intensity of existing linear architectures, many of them are memory-bound — even during training. Without extreme IO optimization, you're basically leaving a huge amount of GPU FLOPs on the table. And inference brings even more challenges than training: How do you deliver a service that is genuinely faster and cheaper? Linear attention has linear compute complexity and constant memory usage. That means there's a crossover point where it becomes more efficient than full attention in compute and memory. In theory, that point lies at a few thousand tokens — which isn't particularly long for today's large models.

But that's just theory. We need to solve a few key problems to actually approach it:

- Low-Precision State Storage: Linear attention is currently far more sensitive to numerical precision than full attention.
- Prefix Caching: In real-world applications, the cache-hit rate for conversations is very high. A new architecture must handle this gracefully.
- Speculative Decoding: How do you optimize speculative decoding with linear attention backbone?

Well fortunately, all of these seem solvable.

## A memory of fixed size

The price of the fixed state can be read straight from the formula. The state is one matrix. Every pair $(k_j, v_j)$ is added into the same $d^2$ numbers, and to recall the value stored under a key, the layer multiplies the state by it:

$$
S^\top k_i = \sum_j (k_j \cdot k_i)\, v_j = (k_i \cdot k_i)\, v_i + \sum_{j \ne i} (k_j \cdot k_i)\, v_j .
$$
The first term is the stored value. The second is interference: every other pair, weighted by how similar its key is to $k_i$. If the keys are orthogonal, the interference is exactly zero, but a $d$-dimensional space has room for only $d$ orthogonal directions.

Beyond that, each new pair blurs the ones already stored. The library has turned into one notebook page on which every note is written over the others; it stays readable while there are few notes.

Softmax attention has no such limit because it never mixes the notes: it keeps them all and lets the exponential pick out the right one. It pays for that with the growing cache. Everything below is about this trade between a fixed state and exact recall.

Arora and colleagues measured it across efficient architectures and called it “a key tradeoff between a model’s state size and recall ability”<sup>[2]</sup>: the smaller the state a model keeps while reading, the worse it recalls.

## II. Why Efficient Attention?

Let's do a thought experiment. If you had infinite compute, would you even bother with linear or sparse attention? Some might bring up theoretical arguments about softmax attention "oversmoothing" in an infinite context... but who knows? Under the current compute bound, no model has truly pushed softmax attention to its absolute limit. So, for all practical purposes, the race for efficient attention is a race to save compute.

For our M2 design, could we aim to save tokens — achieving the same quality with fewer tokens? Well if you believe in scaling laws, to achieve this goal, you'd probably bet on other paths to get there, not efficient attention.

So, the simple truth is this: Compute is finite. We need an architecture that makes better use of it — models that achieve higher performance under the same budget (training & inference).

## Contents

Qwen3-32B, a dense model from April 2025, keeps 32 GiB of keys and values for one conversation of 128 thousand tokens, about half of what its weights take. Qwen3-Next, released by the same team a few months later, keeps 3 GiB at the same length. It doesn’t compress its cache or skip tokens.

Three of every four of its layers simply have no cache: they read the text the way a recurrent network does, into a state of fixed size, and only every fourth layer is ordinary attention.

Qwen3-Next is not the only one. Jamba, the Nemotron-H models, Kimi Linear and, for a while, MiniMax made the same choice: full attention in a few layers, something cheaper in the rest.

This post builds the cheaper part from scratch, from linear attention to the gated delta rule, tests what it can and cannot remember, and then looks at how real models combine the two and what that buys on a GPU.

## What attention remembers

Every attention layer of a Transformer answers the same question for every token: which of the earlier tokens matter here, and what do they say. Softmax attention answers it by brute force. Each token leaves behind a key, which says what it is about, and a value, which says what it contributes.

A new token arrives with a query, compares it with every key, turns the scores into weights with a softmax, and takes the weighted sum of the values:

$$
o_t = \sum_{j \le t} \frac{\exp(q_t \cdot k_j / \sqrt{d})}{\sum_{i \le t} \exp(q_t \cdot k_i / \sqrt{d})}\, v_j .
$$
Nothing is ever thrown away. To write token $t$, the layer needs the keys and values of all $t-1$ tokens before it, which is why serving engines keep them in a *KV cache* instead of recomputing them.

Memory therefore grows linearly with the text, and since each new token reads all of it, reading a whole text of $n$ tokens takes time proportional to $n^2$.

Think of a library that keeps every book it has ever received and checks the whole catalogue for every question. The answers are exact, but the building has to grow with the collection.

## Writing with the delta rule

Plain addition has a second, quieter problem. If the same key comes back with a new value, say a variable that has been reassigned, the state holds the sum of the old and the new value, and reading it returns a mixture of both. Nothing in the notebook can be crossed out.

The remedy dates from 1960, when Widrow and Hoff trained their linear neurons with what became known as the delta rule: compare the output with the target and move the weights in proportion to the error<sup>[3]</sup>.

Schlag, Irie and Schmidhuber noticed that the state of linear attention is a weight matrix, written at every step, and proposed writing it the same way<sup>[4]</sup>. Before storing $v_t$ under $k_t$, read what is already there, and write only the difference:

with $k_t$ of unit length and $\beta_t \in (0, 1)$, a writing strength the layer computes for each token. This is one step of gradient descent on the memory’s error for this key, $\tfrac12 \lVert S^\top k_t - v_t \rVert^2$, with learning rate $\beta_t$: the gradient with respect to $S$ is $k_t (S^\top k_t - v_t)^\top$.

With $\beta_t = 1$, the old value under $k_t$ is erased and the new one is stored exactly. A layer that writes this way is called *DeltaNet*. In the space of values, one write looks like this:


Side by side, the three memories differ in what they keep and in how a new pair changes it:


How much of a difference does editing make? A small experiment shows both sides of it: a $64 \times 64$ memory, random unit keys and values, written once by adding and once by the delta rule, and read back by finding the nearest stored value. Softmax attention, which keeps every pair, is the reference.


The left panel holds a surprise: from 64 pairs on, plain addition recalls more than the delta rule. With $\beta_t = 1$, each write makes the memory return exactly $v_t$ for $k_t$, and since random keys are not orthogonal, it also shifts what the memory returns for every older key that overlaps with $k_t$.

## Hybrids in practice

The first large hybrid was Jamba from AI21, in March 2024: Mamba layers with one attention layer in every eight<sup>[14]</sup>. MiniMax, NVIDIA, Qwen and Moonshot followed, each with its own recurrent layer and its own ratio.

Qwen3-Next uses Gated DeltaNet in three layers out of four. According to the Qwen team, at this ratio “the model consistently outperforms any monolithic architecture”<sup>[17]</sup>.

Kimi Linear uses Kimi Delta Attention, the variant with a gate for every channel, also at 3:1. It leaves word order entirely to the recurrent layers: its attention layers use no positional encoding at all<sup>[9]</sup>.

## III. The Real Bottlenecks

To build a model that can practically be deployed and used by the community, we have to start with what users care: Quality, Speed (TPS), and Price. Quality is non-negotiable. A useless model is useless even if it's free. So how do we make a Linear/Sparse/Hybrid Attention model that performs well enough? The biggest challenge here isn't the architecture design — the real bottleneck is the limitations of evaluation. (As for speed and price, those are heavily influenced by the inference stack—and great models tend to attract great engineers to optimize them.)

### The Evaluation Trap: Goodhart's Law in Action

“As long as you build the benchmark, I'll find a way to beat it.” Over the past few years of LLM development, the pace of leaderboard progress is staggering. No matter how hard a benchmark is — even if the SOTA score starts in single digits — once it catches the industry's attention, it's usually crushed within a few iterations. But how do you build an evaluation system that is comprehensive and actually reflects a model's true capabilities? That's one of the hardest — and most critical — problems in LLM development, and it becomes even more acute when you start messing with a component as fundamental as attention.
### Benchmarks are a Leaky Abstraction

There's no free lunch. When you reduce the complexity of attention, you pay a price. The question is, where?

When we were developing MiniMax-Text-01, everyone was still evaluating MMLU, BBH, MATH, and LongBench (all of which are now saturated). From the perspective of a year ago, a hybrid of Lightning Attention and Full Attention looked just as good as pure full attention. Our own small-scale hybrid models confirmed this on the leaderboards. (Did we find a free lunch?)

Not quite. The price paid became obvious at a larger scale: the model had clear deficits in complex, multi-hop reasoning tasks.

Okay, once a problem is exposed, you can fix it. We developed proxy metrics for this specific weakness and iterated until the hybrid model seemed to match MHA. But does that proxy metric still correlate with real-world downstream performance at an even larger scale? Are there other hidden weaknesses? Who knows. We haven't run those experiments yet.

The better the models get, the harder they are to evaluate. But that's a must part of the journey — keep it up, eval teams!

## When a hybrid is the right choice

A hybrid pays off when contexts are long and there are many of them: agents that carry long transcripts of tool calls, reasoning models that write tens of thousands of tokens, questions over long documents, a server holding hundreds of such conversations at once.

There the cache is most of the memory and reading it is most of the decoding time, and cutting it by a factor of four to ten changes how many users one GPU can serve.

At short contexts the gain is smaller than the headlines suggest. According to Qwen, the decoding throughput of Qwen3-Next is nearly 4 times that of Qwen3-32B at 4K tokens and over 10 times beyond 32K<sup>[17]</sup>.

But Qwen3-Next activates 3 billion parameters per token and Qwen3-32B all 32 billion, so the comparison mixes two savings, the mixture of experts and the hybrid, and the blog doesn’t separate them. The hybrid’s share is the part that grows with the context.

The costs are of three kinds. The first is quality on the tasks attention is best at, precise retrieval and multi-hop reasoning over long inputs: the deficits that sent MiniMax back to full attention.

The second is engineering. Recurrent layers need their own kernels, and serving tricks built around a cache of separate tokens get harder when part of the model keeps a state that has absorbed all of them.

Reusing the cache of a shared prompt needs copies of the state saved at chosen positions, and rolling back a rejected speculative token needs the state from a step earlier.

The third is that the field keeps moving. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next replaced the full attention layers of its hybrid with sparse attention<sup>[23]</sup>, and DeepSeek-V4 combines two kinds of compressed attention instead of adding recurrent layers<sup>[24]</sup>. Both directions go after the same cache.

A hybrid’s way is to give most layers a memory of fixed size and to keep a few that can still read every token.

## A test of memory: associative recall

The language modelling loss says little about memory, because much of predicting the next word needs little of it. A more direct test asks a model to remember what it was told. In multi-query associative recall, a sequence lists key-value pairs and then asks for the values of the keys in a shuffled order<sup>[11]</sup>:

```
k1 v1  k2 v2  ...  kN vN   |   q1 a1  q2 a2  ...  qN aN
```
Each $q_i$ is one of the keys, and the model must put the right value after it. It is the skill behind answering a question about a long document, using a name defined forty pages earlier, or calling a function with the arguments described at the top of a prompt.

I trained six small models on it, each with four layers of width 64 and two heads, the same in everything except how their layers mix tokens: softmax attention in all four, linear attention, DeltaNet, Gated DeltaNet, and two hybrids with three Gated DeltaNet layers and one softmax attention layer.

In one hybrid the attention layer is second; in the other it is on top, the place it has in each block of four in Qwen3-Next.

Every layer, attention included, first passes its queries, keys and values through a short convolution over the last four positions, as Mamba and DeltaNet do, so that a value can carry its key with it.

Each model saw 64 fresh random sequences at each of 4,000 steps and was scored on held-out ones. The models with Gated DeltaNet layers trained on an Apple M2, the others on a T4 (code).


The Transformer recalls every value at every size on the chart. The three recurrent models hold up while there are few pairs and fall apart between 8 and 32: at 32 pairs DeltaNet recalls 36% of the values, linear attention 26% and Gated DeltaNet 2%, and at 64 the best of them, DeltaNet, recalls 13%.

Each head here works with keys of 32 numbers, so by the bound from earlier its state holds at most 32 pairs exactly, and at 16 pairs all three are already well short of full recall.

At 128 pairs even the Transformer didn’t learn the task in 4,000 steps, which is why the chart stops at 64.

## Why one layer of attention is enough

Attention solves associative recall in one layer: the query for $k_i$ meets the stored key $k_i$, the softmax puts nearly all the weight on it, and out comes $v_i$, however many pairs came before.

Arora and colleagues proved that attention needs a model dimension independent of the sequence length for this, while the gated convolutions they studied need one that grows with it.

Measuring the gap in quality between the two kinds of models on real text, they found that “82% of the gap is explained by each model’s ability to recall information that is previously mentioned in-context”<sup>[11]</sup>.

Copying gives the same picture. Jelassi and colleagues proved that two layers of attention can copy strings of exponential length, while models with a fixed state are “fundamentally limited by their fixed-size latent state”<sup>[12]</sup>.

None of this requires attention everywhere. Much of predicting the next token is local, or a matter of keeping a running summary of what the text is about, and a gated recurrent layer does that well and cheaply.

Exact lookups into the distant past are rarer, and a layer that can make them serves the whole model: the recurrent layers around it carry the local context, the attention layer finds the match. In the library picture, most floors work from a notebook page, and every few floors someone is allowed into the archive.

The authors of Mamba-2 tried such hybrids and described the division of labour the same way:

 Attention layers act as a retrieval mechanism to quickly refer to previous tokens in the sequence instead of forcing the model to compress all the context to its memory.

Tri Dao and Albert Gu, the authors of Mamba-2


They found that “around 10% of the total number of layers being attention performs best”<sup>[7]</sup>.

A study at NVIDIA trained an 8-billion-parameter Transformer, pure Mamba and Mamba-2 models and a hybrid with 4 attention layers out of 56 on the same data.

The pure Mamba models began to fail at looking up a number in a phone book beyond about 500 tokens. The hybrid exceeded the Transformer on all 12 standard tasks the authors evaluated, by 2.65 points on average<sup>[13]</sup>.

## IV. What's Next

Scaling remains the name of the game, and context scaling is one of the key problems. Longer and longer context length is key in both pre-training and post-training. As GPU compute growth slows while data length keeps increasing, the benefits of linear and sparse attention will gradually emerge. We should start preparing now:

- Better Data: More multimodal, information-rich long-context data.
- Better Evaluation: More informative evaluation system and experimental paradigms to speed up iteration.
- Better Infrastructure: Mature training and inference infrastructure to fully squeeze out GPU potential.

## V. Addendum: the SWA code...

We accidentally left the SWA inference code in the open-source release, and some people asked why it wasn't used in the final model. Simple answer: the performance wasn't good enough.

That experiment was from quite early on, before GPT-OSS was open-sourced (we were pretty surprised to see its structure, by the way). But I can share a brief summary of our failed attempt. We tried adapting CPT into a Hybrid SWA, testing both inter & intra-layer mixing. The motivation for intra-layer mixing was to balance the compute intensity across all layers, which is friendly to both PP in training and PP or AFD during inference. Unfortunately, neither worked. Performance degraded noticeably as context length grew — which is unacceptable in agentic scenarios.

Our analysis showed that many global attention patterns (like retrieval head and induction head) were already established early during pre-training. CPT can hardly adjust those patterns afterwards. You surely can mitigate the issue by using data probes to identify and keep those heads as full attention — but unfortunately, it's nearly impossible to discover them all from human priors.

(And no, this issue isn't related to attention sinks.)

If you're interested in this line of research, I recommend taking a closer look at GPT-OSS, CWM, and Gemma, especially their long-context performance.

## What it costs on a GPU

The recurrent layer pays off only where the cache grows large, and a single layer on one GPU shows where that starts.

I timed one layer with 16 heads of 128 dimensions, about the size of a Gated DeltaNet layer in Qwen3-Next, in two situations: reading a prompt of $n$ tokens at once, and writing one new token after $n$ tokens.

Softmax attention runs through PyTorch’s fused attention kernel in half precision. Gated DeltaNet runs my plain-PyTorch chunked version in single precision, a Python loop over chunks of 64. The comparison is tilted against the recurrent layer on purpose: if it wins anyway, it wins on arithmetic, not on engineering.



Reading a prompt, softmax attention is faster up to 8K tokens, which is no surprise: its kernel is one fused program, and mine is a loop. The slopes differ, though.

From 512 to 65,536 tokens, a sequence 128 times longer, the attention layer gets 8,600 times slower and the recurrent one 124 times slower. The curves cross between 8K and 16K tokens, and at 65K the recurrent layer is 4.2 times faster.

Writing a token is where the cache costs most. Attention reads the keys and values of every earlier token, 512 MiB at 65K tokens in this one layer, and its time grows in proportion, from 0.08 ms to 3.7 ms. The recurrent layer updates a state of 1 MiB and takes 0.2 ms at any length; at that size the time is mostly the overhead of launching a few small GPU kernels.

From about 2K tokens on, the recurrent step is faster, and at 65K it is 16 times faster.

On one GPU the recurrent layer overtakes attention from about 2K tokens when writing a token, and between 8K and 16K tokens when reading a prompt.

One layer and one sequence understate the difference in a real server. There, the caches of all the conversations in a batch have to fit in memory at once, so a model whose cache is a quarter or an eighth of the size can serve proportionally more conversations at the same length.

Kimi Linear’s 6.3 times, quoted above, comes from exactly that. The attention layers of a hybrid still pay the full price; three quarters of its layers stop paying it.

Both forms compute the same numbers, only in a different order. In code, the recurrent form loops over positions and the parallel one builds the masked score matrix:

```
def linear_recurrent(q, k, v):
    q, k = feature(q), feature(k)
    state = q.new_zeros(*q.shape[:2], q.shape[-1], v.shape[-1])  # S = sum of k v^T
    norm = q.new_zeros(*q.shape[:2], q.shape[-1])                # z = sum of k
    out = []
    for t in range(q.shape[2]):
        state = state + k[:, :, t, :, None] * v[:, :, t, None, :]
        norm = norm + k[:, :, t]
        out.append(torch.einsum("bhk,bhkv->bhv", q[:, :, t], state)
                   / torch.einsum("bhk,bhk->bh", q[:, :, t], norm)[..., None])
    return torch.stack(out, dim=2)
def linear_attention(q, k, v):
    q, k = feature(q), feature(k)
    causal = torch.ones(q.shape[2], q.shape[2], dtype=torch.bool).tril()
    scores = (q @ k.transpose(-1, -2)).masked_fill(~causal, 0)
    return (scores @ v) / scores.sum(-1, keepdim=True)
```
On random inputs in double precision the two functions agree to about $10^{-15}$, which is rounding error. The recurrent form is how the layer writes text, one token at a time; the parallel form is how it trains, all positions at once.

The parallel form also shows a catch: it still builds an $n \times n$ matrix of scores, because with a causal mask every position needs its own prefix of the sum and the brackets can’t simply move. Training a linear layer efficiently needs a third form, which comes later.

### The High Cost of Knowing Things

For complex reasoning tasks, we can sometimes find early proxy metrics that correlate well with final performance — but not for all tasks (at least, not yet). As tasks get harder, the amount of experiment compute required just to get a statistically significant signal on your metric grows astronomically — which is ironic, since we study efficient attention because compute is limited.

And beyond the academic benchmarks, optimization issues often only surface at scale. You never really know what's going to happen until you scale up. Anyone who read our M1 paper will recall the serious precision issues we hit during RL training — problems that would've been spotted earlier. Going back and analyzing Lightning Attention's numerical convergence with that experience in hand was incredibly clarifying. Discovering the real problems is often far harder than solving them.

### A Symphony of Variables

There are just too many variables in model training. Different architectures behave very differently on different data distributions and with different optimizers. In a world where our data is constantly being updated, an experiment run on last month's data mix might yield the opposite conclusion today.

We can't observe everything perfectly — but we're working on finding more reliable experimental strategies.

### Infrastructure: Where Theory Meets Metal

Compared to full attention, the infrastructure for linear and sparse attention is much less mature. To actually get the promised results, there's still a lot of groundwork to fill in.

Take linear attention for example: If you analyze the compute intensity of existing linear architectures, many of them are memory-bound — even during training. Without extreme IO optimization, you're basically leaving a huge amount of GPU FLOPs on the table. And inference brings even more challenges than training: How do you deliver a service that is genuinely faster and cheaper? Linear attention has linear compute complexity and constant memory usage. That means there's a crossover point where it becomes more efficient than full attention in compute and memory. In theory, that point lies at a few thousand tokens — which isn't particularly long for today's large models.

But that's just theory. We need to solve a few key problems to actually approach it:

- Low-Precision State Storage: Linear attention is currently far more sensitive to numerical precision than full attention.
- Prefix Caching: In real-world applications, the cache-hit rate for conversations is very high. A new architecture must handle this gracefully.
- Speculative Decoding: How do you optimize speculative decoding with linear attention backbone?

Well fortunately, all of these seem solvable.

## A memory of fixed size

The price of the fixed state can be read straight from the formula. The state is one matrix. Every pair $(k_j, v_j)$ is added into the same $d^2$ numbers, and to recall the value stored under a key, the layer multiplies the state by it:

$$
S^\top k_i = \sum_j (k_j \cdot k_i)\, v_j = (k_i \cdot k_i)\, v_i + \sum_{j \ne i} (k_j \cdot k_i)\, v_j .
$$
The first term is the stored value. The second is interference: every other pair, weighted by how similar its key is to $k_i$. If the keys are orthogonal, the interference is exactly zero, but a $d$-dimensional space has room for only $d$ orthogonal directions.

Beyond that, each new pair blurs the ones already stored. The library has turned into one notebook page on which every note is written over the others; it stays readable while there are few notes.

Softmax attention has no such limit because it never mixes the notes: it keeps them all and lets the exponential pick out the right one. It pays for that with the growing cache. Everything below is about this trade between a fixed state and exact recall.

Arora and colleagues measured it across efficient architectures and called it “a key tradeoff between a model’s state size and recall ability”<sup>[2]</sup>: the smaller the state a model keeps while reading, the worse it recalls.

## II. Why Efficient Attention?

Let's do a thought experiment. If you had infinite compute, would you even bother with linear or sparse attention? Some might bring up theoretical arguments about softmax attention "oversmoothing" in an infinite context... but who knows? Under the current compute bound, no model has truly pushed softmax attention to its absolute limit. So, for all practical purposes, the race for efficient attention is a race to save compute.

For our M2 design, could we aim to save tokens — achieving the same quality with fewer tokens? Well if you believe in scaling laws, to achieve this goal, you'd probably bet on other paths to get there, not efficient attention.

So, the simple truth is this: Compute is finite. We need an architecture that makes better use of it — models that achieve higher performance under the same budget (training & inference).

## Contents

Qwen3-32B, a dense model from April 2025, keeps 32 GiB of keys and values for one conversation of 128 thousand tokens, about half of what its weights take. Qwen3-Next, released by the same team a few months later, keeps 3 GiB at the same length. It doesn’t compress its cache or skip tokens.

Three of every four of its layers simply have no cache: they read the text the way a recurrent network does, into a state of fixed size, and only every fourth layer is ordinary attention.

Qwen3-Next is not the only one. Jamba, the Nemotron-H models, Kimi Linear and, for a while, MiniMax made the same choice: full attention in a few layers, something cheaper in the rest.

This post builds the cheaper part from scratch, from linear attention to the gated delta rule, tests what it can and cannot remember, and then looks at how real models combine the two and what that buys on a GPU.

## What attention remembers

Every attention layer of a Transformer answers the same question for every token: which of the earlier tokens matter here, and what do they say. Softmax attention answers it by brute force. Each token leaves behind a key, which says what it is about, and a value, which says what it contributes.

A new token arrives with a query, compares it with every key, turns the scores into weights with a softmax, and takes the weighted sum of the values:

$$
o_t = \sum_{j \le t} \frac{\exp(q_t \cdot k_j / \sqrt{d})}{\sum_{i \le t} \exp(q_t \cdot k_i / \sqrt{d})}\, v_j .
$$
Nothing is ever thrown away. To write token $t$, the layer needs the keys and values of all $t-1$ tokens before it, which is why serving engines keep them in a *KV cache* instead of recomputing them.

Memory therefore grows linearly with the text, and since each new token reads all of it, reading a whole text of $n$ tokens takes time proportional to $n^2$.

Think of a library that keeps every book it has ever received and checks the whole catalogue for every question. The answers are exact, but the building has to grow with the collection.

## Writing with the delta rule

Plain addition has a second, quieter problem. If the same key comes back with a new value, say a variable that has been reassigned, the state holds the sum of the old and the new value, and reading it returns a mixture of both. Nothing in the notebook can be crossed out.

The remedy dates from 1960, when Widrow and Hoff trained their linear neurons with what became known as the delta rule: compare the output with the target and move the weights in proportion to the error<sup>[3]</sup>.

Schlag, Irie and Schmidhuber noticed that the state of linear attention is a weight matrix, written at every step, and proposed writing it the same way<sup>[4]</sup>. Before storing $v_t$ under $k_t$, read what is already there, and write only the difference:
